shorts.title: The Chocolate Bar That Melted: The Microwave Oven
shorts.covers: An engineer working on radar in 1945 noticed the chocolate bar in his pocket had melted, and invented the microwave oven.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

script.title: The Microwave Oven: The Melted Chocolate Bar
script.description: In 1945 an engineer working on radar equipment noticed the chocolate bar in his pocket had melted. He tried popcorn next, and invented the microwave oven.

shorts.title: Jenner and the Milkmaids
shorts.covers: Edward Jenner noticed milkmaids who caught cowpox did not get smallpox, and in 1796 tested his idea on a boy called James Phipps.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

script.title: Jenner and the Milkmaids
script.description: A country doctor heard that milkmaids who caught a mild cow disease never caught smallpox. In 1796 he tested the idea on a boy, and invented the first vaccine.

shorts.title: The Dog Who Orbited the Earth
shorts.covers: In 1957 the Soviet Union sent a stray dog called Laika into orbit, and the story of what happened to her stayed secret for decades.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

script.title: Laika: The Dog Who Orbited the Earth
script.description: In 1957 a stray dog from the streets of Moscow became the first animal to orbit the Earth. For decades the world was told she lived for days. The truth came out in 2002.

shorts.title: The Fish That Came Back From Extinction
shorts.covers: In 1938 a museum curator in South Africa spotted a strange blue fish on a fishing boat, a coelacanth, thought extinct for 66 million years.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

script.title: The Fish That Came Back From Extinction
script.description: In 1938 a young museum curator in South Africa spotted a strange blue fish on a trawler. Scientists thought it had died out 66 million years ago.

shorts.title: Who Invented the Light Bulb?
shorts.covers: Edison is remembered, but dozens of inventors raced to make a bulb that lasted, and the real story is about the filament.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

script.title: Who Really Invented the Light Bulb?
script.description: Everybody says Edison. But for decades, dozens of inventors had made bulbs that glowed. The real race was to find a thread that would not burn out.

shorts.title: Eratosthenes Measures the Earth
shorts.covers: Around 240 BC a librarian in Egypt measured the size of the whole Earth using a stick's shadow and a camel journey.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

script.title: Eratosthenes Measures the Earth
script.description: Over two thousand years ago, a librarian in Egypt worked out the size of the whole planet. All he needed was a stick, the sun, and the distance to another town.

shorts.title: Why Is the Sky Blue?
shorts.covers: The answer came from a Victorian scientist working out how sunlight scatters off the tiny molecules of air.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

script.title: Why Is the Sky Blue?
script.description: Sunlight is white, so why is the sky blue and the sunset red? A Victorian lord worked it out on paper, and the answer is the air itself.

shorts.title: The Man Who Breathed Laughing Gas
shorts.covers: In 1799 a young Humphry Davy breathed nitrous oxide in Bristol, wrote about the giggles, and missed that it could stop pain.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

script.title: The Man Who Breathed Laughing Gas
script.description: In 1799 a twenty-year-old chemist breathed a strange gas from a silk bag, laughed, and wrote that it might stop pain in surgery. Then nobody tried it for forty-four years.

shorts.title: The Year Without a Summer
shorts.covers: In 1815 a volcano erupted in Indonesia, and the next summer snow fell in June in America and crops failed across Europe.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

script.title: The Year Without a Summer
script.description: In June 1816 snow fell in New England and crops failed across Europe. The cause was a volcano on an island halfway round the world, and it took a century to connect them.

shorts.title: The Antikythera Mechanism
shorts.covers: In 1901 divers found a lump of corroded bronze in a Greek shipwreck, and it turned out to be a 2,000-year-old astronomical computer.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

script.title: The Antikythera Mechanism
script.description: Divers found a lump of green bronze in a Greek shipwreck. It took a hundred years to see it was a computer.

shorts.title: The Glowing Screen: Rontgen and X-Rays
shorts.covers: In 1895 Wilhelm Rontgen saw a screen glow across his dark lab, and days later took the first X-ray, of his wife's hand.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

script.title: The Glowing Screen: Rontgen and X-Rays
script.description: In 1895 a screen began to glow across a dark lab in Germany. Weeks later, a woman saw the bones of her own hand.

shorts.title: The Day Surgery Stopped Hurting
shorts.covers: In 1846, in front of a packed theatre in Boston, a dentist put a patient to sleep with ether, and the surgeon cut without a scream.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Gagarin's 108 Minutes
shorts.covers: In 1961 a former foundry worker became the first person in space, and landed by parachute in a field in front of a startled farmer.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Jane Goodall and the Termite Fishing Chimp
shorts.covers: In 1960 a young Englishwoman in Tanzania watched a chimpanzee strip a twig to fish for termites, and changed what we thought made humans special.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Telephone and the Race to the Patent Office
shorts.covers: Alexander Graham Bell filed his telephone patent on the same day in 1876 as a rival, and the argument lasted for years.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Zero: The Number That Was Nothing
shorts.covers: How Indian mathematicians turned nothing into a number, and how it travelled to Europe.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Archimedes and the Bath
shorts.covers: The story of how a Greek scientist worked out whether the king's crown was pure gold, and ran down the street shouting eureka.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Pavlov's Dogs
shorts.covers: A Russian scientist studying digestion noticed his dogs drooled before the food arrived, and discovered learned reflexes.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: How We Learned to Forecast the Weather
shorts.covers: After a storm sank a ship in 1859, Robert FitzRoy started the first public weather forecasts, and was mocked when they were wrong.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: How the Pyramids Were Built
shorts.covers: What archaeologists have found about the workers, ramps and tools that built the Great Pyramid, from their own villages and notes.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Sweet Hands: How Saccharin Was Found
shorts.covers: In 1879 a chemist forgot to wash his hands before dinner, noticed his bread tasted sweet, and traced it back to his experiment.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Lister and the Clean Operation
shorts.covers: Joseph Lister read Pasteur's work on germs and started spraying carbolic acid in his operating theatre in Glasgow, and his patients stopped dying.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Apollo 13: Successful Failure
shorts.covers: In 1970 an oxygen tank exploded on the way to the Moon, and the crew and engineers had to improvise a way home with a lunar lander.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: How Bats See in the Dark
shorts.covers: An Italian priest in the 1790s blindfolded bats and plugged their ears, and the answer took 150 years and a microphone to confirm.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Barcode: Lines Drawn in the Sand
shorts.covers: In 1948 an engineer on a Miami beach dragged his fingers through the sand and drew the idea for the barcode.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Longitude Prize
shorts.covers: Ships kept running aground because sailors could not work out how far east or west they were, until a carpenter built a clock that kept time at sea.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Galileo and the Leaning Tower
shorts.covers: Did Galileo really drop balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa? What he actually did, and why heavy and light things fall together.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Benjamin Franklin's Daylight Saving Joke
shorts.covers: How a joke letter about Parisians sleeping late turned, over a century later, into changing the clocks.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Ozone Hole
shorts.covers: In 1985 British scientists in Antarctica found a hole in the ozone layer, and the world banned the chemicals causing it.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Reading the Rosetta Stone
shorts.covers: In 1822 Jean-Francois Champollion cracked Egyptian hieroglyphs using a stone with the same text in three scripts.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Superglue: The Failure That Stuck
shorts.covers: A chemist trying to make clear plastic gun sights in 1942 found a liquid that stuck to everything, and only years later saw what it was good for.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Insulin: The Dogs, the Doctor and the Dying Children
shorts.covers: In 1922 in Toronto, a young surgeon and his student found a way to treat diabetes, and children close to death woke up.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Hidden Figures: The Women Who Did the Maths
shorts.covers: Before electronic computers, a group of Black women mathematicians at NASA calculated the paths that took astronauts into orbit.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Dance of the Honeybees
shorts.covers: Karl von Frisch discovered that honeybees tell each other where flowers are by dancing a figure of eight.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The World Wide Web: Tim Berners-Lee's Proposal
shorts.covers: In 1989 a scientist at CERN wrote a proposal his boss called vague but exciting, and it became the web.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Codebreakers of Bletchley Park
shorts.covers: How mathematicians and crossword solvers in a country house broke the German Enigma code in the Second World War.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: How Rainbows Work
shorts.covers: Isaac Newton split sunlight with a prism in a darkened room and showed that white light is made of every colour.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Scientist Who Infected Himself With Yellow Fever
shorts.covers: In 1900 a team in Cuba proved mosquitoes spread yellow fever, and one of them died proving it.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Eruption of Vesuvius
shorts.covers: In AD 79 a volcano buried Pompeii, and a young Roman called Pliny wrote down what he saw from across the bay.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Roman Concrete That Gets Stronger
shorts.covers: Why Roman harbour walls still stand after 2,000 years in the sea, while modern concrete crumbles in decades.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Glass That Did Not Shatter
shorts.covers: In 1903 a French chemist dropped a glass flask that cracked but held together, because a plastic coating had dried inside it. It became safety glass.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Stethoscope: A Rolled-Up Piece of Paper
shorts.covers: In 1816 a French doctor too embarrassed to put his ear to a young woman's chest rolled a sheet of paper into a tube, and heard her heart clearly.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Hubble Telescope's Blurry Start
shorts.covers: In 1990 the most expensive telescope ever launched sent back blurry pictures, because a mirror was ground wrong by a hair's width.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Peppered Moth
shorts.covers: During the Industrial Revolution, soot turned Britain's tree trunks black, and black moths took over. It became famous evidence of natural selection.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Toilet That Flushed: Victorian London's Great Stink
shorts.covers: In the hot summer of 1858 the stench of the Thames shut Parliament, and Joseph Bazalgette built the sewers that saved London.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Ada Lovelace and the First Program
shorts.covers: In 1843 Ada Lovelace wrote notes on a machine that was never built, including what is now called the first computer program.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Einstein's Miracle Year
shorts.covers: In 1905 a patent clerk in Switzerland published four papers that changed physics, including the most famous equation in the world.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Sir Isaac Newton's Needle
shorts.covers: To understand colour, Newton pushed a blunt needle around the back of his own eye and recorded what he saw.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Tsunami: The Girl Who Knew the Signs
shorts.covers: In 2004 a ten-year-old British girl on a beach in Thailand remembered a geography lesson, and saved about a hundred people.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Library of Alexandria
shorts.covers: What the greatest library of the ancient world held, and how it really disappeared.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Goodyear and the Hot Stove
shorts.covers: Charles Goodyear spent years and all his money trying to make rubber stop melting, until a mixture of rubber and sulphur dropped on a hot stove.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Dorothy Hodgkin Solves the Shapes of Medicines
shorts.covers: Using X-rays and years of patient work, Dorothy Hodgkin worked out the shape of penicillin, vitamin B12 and insulin.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Voyager's Golden Record
shorts.covers: In 1977 two spacecraft left Earth carrying a golden record of music, greetings and sounds, in case anyone ever finds them.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Deep Sea Vents
shorts.covers: In 1977 scientists diving off the Galapagos found hot springs on the sea floor, and life thriving there with no sunlight at all.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Who Invented the Bicycle?
shorts.covers: From a wooden running machine in 1817 to the chain-driven safety bicycle, it took seventy years to make a bike anyone could ride.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Florence Nightingale's Chart
shorts.covers: Florence Nightingale used a new kind of chart to show that more soldiers died from dirty hospitals than from battle wounds.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Speed of Light, Measured
shorts.covers: In 1676 a Danish astronomer noticed Jupiter's moons were late, and worked out that light takes time to travel.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Mendel's Peas
shorts.covers: A monk in a monastery garden in Brno crossed thousands of pea plants and discovered the laws of inheritance, and nobody noticed for 35 years.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Why Earthquakes Happen
shorts.covers: How a scientist studying the 1906 San Francisco earthquake worked out that rock bends like a spring and then snaps.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Stonehenge: Moving the Stones
shorts.covers: How the builders of Stonehenge moved giant stones from Wales, more than 200 kilometres away, 5,000 years ago.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Heartbeat Mistake: The Pacemaker
shorts.covers: In 1956 an engineer fitted the wrong resistor to a heart rhythm recorder, heard a steady pulse, and realised he had made a pacemaker.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The First Heart Transplant
shorts.covers: In 1967 in Cape Town, Christiaan Barnard's team put a donor's heart into a dying man, and the world held its breath.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Pluto: The Planet That Was Demoted
shorts.covers: Pluto was found by a farm boy in 1930, and in 2006 astronomers voted it out of the list of planets.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Elephants That Talk Through the Ground
shorts.covers: How researchers discovered elephants talk to each other with rumbles too low for human ears, carried for miles through the ground.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Fridge: Keeping Food Cold Without Ice
shorts.covers: How scientists learned to move heat with gas and pressure, and replaced the iceman who once delivered blocks of ice.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Metre: Measuring the World in the Revolution
shorts.covers: During the French Revolution two astronomers spent seven years measuring a line from Dunkirk to Barcelona to define the metre.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Why Do Things Glow When Hot?
shorts.covers: A problem about the colour of hot metal led Max Planck in 1900 to the strange idea that energy comes in little packets.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Miller-Urey Experiment
shorts.covers: In 1952 two chemists sent sparks through a flask of gases and water, and made the building blocks of life.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Gulf Stream: A River in the Ocean
shorts.covers: Benjamin Franklin noticed mail ships from England took weeks longer than merchant ships, and mapped a river of warm water in the Atlantic.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Baghdad Battery
shorts.covers: A clay jar with a copper tube inside was found near Baghdad, and people have argued for decades about whether it made electricity.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Mauve: The Colour Made From Coal Tar
shorts.covers: In 1856 an eighteen-year-old trying to make a malaria drug made a purple dye instead, and started the modern chemical industry.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Polio and the Sugar Cube
shorts.covers: How Jonas Salk's injection and Albert Sabin's drops on a sugar cube took polio from a terror of every summer to the edge of extinction.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Landing on a Comet
shorts.covers: In 2014 a probe the size of a washing machine landed on a speeding comet after a ten-year journey, and bounced.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Tree Network Under the Forest
shorts.covers: How a Canadian forest scientist found trees sharing food and signals through fungi in the soil.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Printing Press
shorts.covers: Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg combined movable metal letters, oil ink and a wine press, and books became affordable.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Pi: The Never-Ending Number
shorts.covers: How mathematicians chased the digits of pi for 4,000 years, from ancient Babylon to supercomputers.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Experiment That Showed Light Was a Wave
shorts.covers: In 1801 Thomas Young shone light through two slits and saw stripes on the wall, and the result is still strange today.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Cavendish Experiment: Weighing the Earth
shorts.covers: In 1798 a shy scientist used lead balls and a wire in a shed to weigh the whole planet.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Snowflakes: No Two Alike
shorts.covers: A Vermont farmer called Wilson Bentley photographed more than 5,000 snowflakes from 1885, and never found two the same.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Damascus Steel
shorts.covers: Swords from the medieval Middle East held a sharp edge and a wavy pattern, and the method was lost for centuries.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Slinky: A Spring That Walked
shorts.covers: In 1943 a naval engineer knocked a spring off a shelf, watched it walk down a stack of books, and turned it into a toy.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Doctor Who Swallowed Bacteria
shorts.covers: Nobody believed stomach ulcers were caused by germs, so in 1984 an Australian doctor drank a dish of bacteria to prove it.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The First Picture of a Black Hole
shorts.covers: In 2019 telescopes around the world worked together as one Earth-sized dish to photograph the shadow of a black hole.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Why Dodos Disappeared
shorts.covers: The dodo lived safely on Mauritius until sailors arrived in 1598, and within a century there were none left.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Photography: The First Picture
shorts.covers: In 1826 a Frenchman pointed a box at his courtyard for hours, and made the oldest surviving photograph.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Seven Bridges of Konigsberg
shorts.covers: In 1736 a puzzle about walking over seven bridges once each led Leonhard Euler to invent a whole new branch of maths.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Why Ice Floats
shorts.covers: Most things shrink when they freeze, but water expands, and that one odd fact keeps lakes and oceans alive.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Michelson and Morley's Failed Experiment
shorts.covers: In 1887 two scientists tried to measure the invisible substance light travelled through, found nothing, and that nothing changed physics.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Greenhouse Effect, Discovered in 1856
shorts.covers: An American scientist called Eunice Foote filled glass jars with different gases, left them in the sun, and found carbon dioxide trapped the most heat.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Ancient Brain Surgery
shorts.covers: Skulls thousands of years old have neat holes drilled in them, and the bone shows many patients survived.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Cosmic Static: The Echo of the Big Bang
shorts.covers: In 1964 two radio astronomers could not get rid of a hiss in their antenna, even after cleaning out pigeon droppings. It was the afterglow of the Big Bang.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Smallpox Hunters
shorts.covers: How a global team tracked down the last cases of smallpox, village by village, until in 1980 it became the first human disease ever wiped out.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Pale Blue Dot
shorts.covers: In 1990, as Voyager 1 left the solar system, it turned round and photographed Earth as a tiny speck in a beam of sunlight.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Monarch Butterfly's Journey
shorts.covers: For decades nobody knew where North America's monarch butterflies went in winter, until a tagging project found the mountain in Mexico.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Smoke Alarm: A Gas Detector That Kept Going Off
shorts.covers: In the 1930s a Swiss physicist trying to build a poison gas detector noticed that cigarette smoke set it off, and the smoke alarm began.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Alan Turing's Question
shorts.covers: In 1950 Alan Turing asked whether machines could think, and suggested a test that is still argued over today.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: The Higgs Boson Hunt
shorts.covers: It took fifty years and the biggest machine ever built to find the particle that gives other particles their mass.

shorts.title: The Slowest Experiment in the World
shorts.covers: In 1927 a professor in Brisbane poured tar pitch into a funnel to show it flows, and a drop falls about once a decade. Nobody has ever seen one fall.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Ball Lightning
shorts.covers: For centuries people reported glowing balls floating through rooms in storms, and in 2012 scientists in China finally recorded one by accident.
shorts.source: Histories of science, the original papers where available, and reputable science journalism

shorts.title: Greek Fire
shorts.covers: The Byzantine Empire had a liquid fire that burned on water and saved Constantinople, and its recipe is still unknown.
